lead: Between fixes, heading, log and clock carry your position forward. Add leeway and stream for an estimated position; turn the triangle round for the course to steer.

sections.title: True on the chart, compass at the helm

blocks.p: **Variation** comes from the chart's rose; **deviation** from the steering compass's card for the heading you are on: read it again for each new heading.

blocks.rule: True to compass: subtract east, add west. Compass to true: the reverse.

blocks.p: By the **1 in 60 rule** one degree of error is a mile off track after 60 miles.

sections.title: Heading, log and clock
refs: Navigation — the log and its error

blocks.p: A **DR position** is the true course steered and the distance run through the water, laid off from the last fix. Distance is speed × time, with time in decimal hours: 1 h 12 min is 1.2 h.
Mark a DR with a line across the track, an EP with a triangle, a fix with a circle, each with its time. Legs on different headings go end to end.

Check the **log**: at slack water it should agree with the SOG; a fouled paddlewheel under-reads. Over a measured distance take the mean speed of two opposite runs. A log showing 2.2 M for 2.0 over-reads: divide by 1.1. If it fails, take speed from the engine revs, not the SOG.

sections.title: Write it down while the plotter works
refs: Navigation — keeping the plot at night

blocks.p: A plot can be rebuilt only from what was written: time, log reading and the heading really steered, each hour and at each alteration, with a position on paper. Then a dead plotter costs an hour of DR, not the night.

In **fog**, slow down and work each stretch at its own speed. Closing a coast blind, aim to one side of the harbour by more than your likely error: then you know which way to turn. Near dangers plot every six minutes: a tenth of the speed.

sections.title: Add leeway, then the stream
refs: Chartwork — ground track and water track

blocks.p: **Leeway** pushes the boat away from the wind: wind on the port side, add it to the heading; on the starboard side, subtract. Greatest close-hauled, nil on a run, it shows as the angle between wake and stern. The result is the **water track**.

From the end of the water track lay off the **tidal stream**: its set, the direction it flows towards, and rate × time. That point is the **EP**; the line from the fix to it is the **ground track**, the one to check against dangers. Arrowheads: water track one, ground track two, stream three.

Take the stream from a tidal diamond or the atlas; each hourly value serves half an hour either side. Interpolate the rate by the day's range, even beyond springs. On your track the diamond beats the atlas.

fig.title: Rate from a diamond
lines: Mean ranges: neaps 2.0 m, springs 5.0 m
Today's range 4.0 m: 2/3 of the way up

blocks.p: Across a stream you aim up-tide. Find the angle by drawing:

list: From your best position, fix or EP, draw the track through the destination.
From the same point lay off the stream for the period.
From its end swing an arc of boat speed for that period to cut the track.
That line is the course to steer; start to cut is the distance made good.

blocks.p: Never join the stream to the destination. If the arc cuts beyond it, rework with the shorter time. A slower boat needs a bigger angle; a stream across the track faster than the boat leaves no answer. Then steer into the wind by the leeway and convert to compass.

For a long crossing lay off every hour's stream end to end and swing one arc for the whole time. On that **one course** the ground track bows down-tide and returns as the stream turns: the shortest way through the water. Do not chase the cross-track error or point at the waypoint; where the curve crosses a danger, work each hour's course.

fig.note: The streams cancel: steer 000°T all the way

sections.title: When you will arrive
refs: Chartwork — speed made good and ETA
Passage making — motor-sailing against the tide

blocks.p: The ETA comes from the speed made good over the ground: the SOG from the triangle, or log speed plus a fair stream, less a foul one. Mind the decimals: 0.4 h is 24 minutes.

fig.title: ETA: worked example
lines: Log 6.0 kn, stream 1.5 kn foul: SOG 4.5 kn
One knot more, SOG 5.5 kn: 2 h 33 min

blocks.p: The plotter's ETA assumes the present SOG lasts: if the stream will turn, work each stretch yourself. Beating, tacks 45° off the bearing make good 0.7 of your speed. Against a foul stream each extra knot counts for more: weigh the time saved against the fuel.

sections.title: COG and SOG include the stream
refs: Navigation — the plotter: heading, COG, SOG
Chartwork — accuracy of DR and EP

blocks.p: Heading and log are through the water; **COG** and **SOG** are over the ground, stream and leeway included. The COG line, not the bow, shows where you are going. Never add the stream to them: it would count twice.

lines: Same direction, 1.3 kn faster: a fair stream

blocks.p: The plotter's own course to steer is just the bearing back to the route, stream ignored. At low speed in a swell COG and SOG jump: use compass and log.

An EP is an area that grows every hour since the fix. At the next fix, read the gap: along the track it is the log or the stream's rate; across it, heading, leeway or set. From a plain DR to the fix is the stream you had: 2.4 M in two hours is 1.2 kn. Restart from the fix.
